analysis.one_liner: Blocks the Education Department's college program 'gainful employment' rule until a full impact analysis and GAO review are done.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Education Department had proposed a 'gainful employment' rule in March 2014 that would cut federal student aid from college career programs whose graduates borrow heavily but don't earn enough to repay it — a rule aimed mainly at for-profit colleges. This bill would bar the Department from finalizing that rule until it published a detailed analysis of the rule's effects on every type of institution and student group, and until the Government Accountability Office reviewed that analysis — adding roughly 90 days or more before the rule could take effect.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be for-profit career colleges, whose enrollment and revenue depend heavily on federal student aid (Title IV loans and Pell Grants) and which faced the biggest cuts under the gainful employment rule. Students currently enrolled in affected programs would see no immediate change.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would block the Secretary of Education from issuing a final rule or implementing the March 25, 2014 proposed gainful employment rule, or any other rule amending the relevant regulations, until 90 days after specified steps are completed.

Before the rule could move, the Secretary would have to publish a complete data analysis of the rule's impact on all postsecondary programs and students — including Pell Grant recipients, minority students, students over 24, and veterans — in a format similar to the Department's 2012 informational rate calculations.
The Comptroller General would also have to issue a report reviewing that analysis for accuracy and completeness before the rule could be finalized.

analysis.who_pays: Students and taxpayers would bear the cost of delay: young people could keep enrolling in — and borrowing federal aid for — career programs that the rule was designed to screen out, programs where graduates often can't repay their loans. Taxpayer dollars and Pell Grant funding would continue flowing to programs that fail the eventual test.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have delayed, by at least 90 days, a rule designed to protect students from career-training programs that leave them with debt they cannot repay; every month of delay lets more students enroll in and borrow for programs that may eventually fail the test.

Supporters argued the Department's gainful employment analyses had been flawed — the bill specifically demands a review for accuracy modeled on the 2012 informational rate calculations — and that institutions of all types, not just for-profits, deserved to see program-level data before a rule cut off their students' aid.

The requirement covers all categories of institutions, so even well-regarded public and nonprofit programs would have been subject to the same heightened analysis process before the rule could take effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — transparent, verified data before a major rule takes effect — is a reasonable process demand, and the analysis it required would have covered students and institutions of all types. But its practical effect was to delay a rule aimed mainly at for-profit colleges, whose federal-aid-funded business model the rule threatened. The added analysis and GAO review could be justified on the merits; the cost falls on the students the rule was meant to protect, who would remain exposed to low-value programs during the delay.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then to its higher-education subcommittee, and never came up for a vote before the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Salmon introduced the bill on June 18, 2014, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On November 17, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training — a step that typically signals a bill is being studied rather than advanced.
No further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, so the bill never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Students and taxpayers benefited from the bill's death, since the gainful employment rule could proceed toward finalization without the added delay. For-profit colleges failed to get the postponement they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Students awaiting the gainful employment rule

for.name: Rep. Matt Salmon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 19 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 27 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support.

for.name: For-profit college industry
for.role: Industry whose federal-aid revenue the gainful employment rule threatened
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for legislation to delay or block the 2014 gainful employment rule.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or floor action on the bill, leaving it in committee.

against.name: Obama Administration / Department of Education
against.role: Agency proposing the gainful employment rule
against.what_they_did: Proposed the gainful employment rule in March 2014 and pushed for its finalization, which the bill would have blocked.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 15 Democrats and 12 Republicans among 27 cosponsors — but no roll-call vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of support on the floor is unknown.

industries.note: The gainful employment rule would cut federal student aid from career programs whose graduates carry heavy debt relative to earnings — a rule aimed squarely at for-profit colleges, which draw much of their revenue from federal aid. This bill would postpone that outcome, protecting the industry's revenue while leaving students enrolled in those programs.

industries.industry: Public and nonprofit colleges with career programs
industries.note: The bill's required analysis would cover programs at all institution types, and some public and nonprofit schools shared concerns about how the rule's debt-to-earnings measures would treat their programs. But the delay primarily benefited the for-profit sector the rule targeted most.
